newsitem.title: UK: Europe's car makers need to cut costs, axe jobs.
newsitem.headline: Europe's car makers need to cut costs, axe jobs.

text.p: Europe's car makers face an endless treadmill of efficiency drives if they are to survive chronic overcapacity and stagnant markets, analysts said Friday.

The future is all about slashing jobs, investing in more efficient ways of building cars to meet soggy demand, cutting prices in the face of competition from low cost Asian producers, then doing it all over again.
Analysts say that of the big six mass car manufacturers in Europe, only Germany's Volkswagen is operating at a sufficient size to ensure long-term viability.
France's Renault and Peugeot need to merge to attain viability, according to one analyst.
News yesterday that Ford of Europe was slashing 1,300 jobs at its Halewood, England, plant is only the tip of the iceberg.
Up to 40,000 jobs are in jeopardy in France, according to analysts. Maybe even more in Germany.

And this in an industry that has already shed 400,000 jobs in the last 10 years. According to the Brussels based industry association ACEA, car manufacturers in western Europe now employ around 1.6 million, down from 2 million in 1987.
During the boom years of the 1980s, car makers were desperate to meet demand which seemed set to grow exponentially.
They invested heavily in the latest technology, only to be slapped down by the biggest sales slump in 50 years.

In 1993 sales dived by more than two million to about 11.5 million. Since then there has been a gradual recovery, but nothing like the heady prospects of up to 17 million a year by the year 2000 that the industry had been banking on.
Manufacturers now fight for every sale, offering discounts and deep price cuts. Governments have helped by offering incentives to replace older, polluting vehicles.

"We can expect more Halewood experiences across Europe, as manufacturers constantly reinvent themselves making efficiencies to keep ahead of the game," said Peter Schmidt, joint managing director of Automotive Industry Data.
Schmidt said changes in lifestyles and fashion have also made it tough for the industry. People, especially Germans, no longer felt the need to buy new cars to impress their friends.
"Now they are saying things like mine is eight years old and still running beautifully," Schmidt said.
Schmidt said that although the problems were huge, he was confident manufucturers would keep on top of the constant drive to cut costs and avoid the final indignity - takeover.
Karl Ludwigsen, chairman of industry consultancy Ludwigsen Associates, is not so sure. "The only European auto company running at a satisfactory scale economy is VW," Ludwigsen said.

VW was west Europe's market leader in 1996 with 17.2 percent market share, way ahead of General Motors Opel and Vauxhall's 12.5 percent and Peugeot (11.9 percent), Ford (11.6 percent), Fiat of Italy (11.2 percent) and Renault (10.1 percent).
"The others are clinging to the margins. Ford and GM are no longer really candidates for consolidation, they're integrating their European operations with their global manufacturing."
"But Fiat and Renault and Peugeot don't have that option and need to look elsewhere for some kind of scale economy to help them compete globally," Ludwigsen said.
France is currently studying a plan to help Renault and Peugeot in mass early retirements to cut costs. French newspapers have said that around 40,000 jobs could be at stake.
"Maybe the French government could push for a Renault Peugeot merger in the light of this? There's certainly not room long-term for two major French producers," Ludwigsen said.
